1:
The great work of the wall opens where sacrifice enters the city, and the witnesses gather first around the high priest who set the example. The reformed John Gill identifies Eliashib as the grandson of Jeshua or Joshua, his father being Joiakim; that the high priest rose first, with his brethren the priests, set a good example to priests and people alike and served to animate and encourage them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch frame the whole register: the enumeration of builders begins with the sheep-gate and the adjoining wall built by the priests, and ends at the same gate with the goldsmiths and merchants of v.32; almost throughout it is said that each party built by the side of the one before, so that the course of the wall is followed and the gates named in their actual order.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the priests' precedence a lesson: ministers should be foremost in every good work, obliged by their office to quicken others by example as well as by doctrine — if there be labour, who so fit to work; if danger, who so fit to venture? The sheep-gate, he explains, was so called because through it were brought the sheep for sacrifice, and therefore the priests, whose inheritance was the offerings made by fire, undertook its repair; and of this gate alone it is said that they sanctified it, either because it led to the temple, or because with it the building began and here they solemnly committed the city and its walls to the divine protection.

On that word sanctified the wesleyan-arminian witnesses press closer. Adam Clarke reads it as consecration: as the returned exiles had begun with sacrifice as soon as they had an altar, it was proper that the gate through which the victims entered should be set apart for that use only. John Wesley weighs the Hebrew, granting that the word sometimes means merely prepared or repaired, yet judging the common rendering best, since it is said of this gate alone; being built by the priests and nearest the temple, it might in a peculiar manner be sanctified by solemn prayer and sacrifice, and so dedicated to God's service. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the topography: the sheep gate lay in the neighbourhood of the priests' quarter, and through it the victims passed to sacrifice, first being washed in the neighbouring pool of Bethesda; its sanctification was an earnest of the later consecration of the whole wall. The witnesses do not divide over the fact — priests leading, sacrifice entering, the first gate hallowed — only over whether sanctified names a mere repairing or a true dedication, and the weight of them falls on dedication.
2:
Next to the priests came a company of countrymen, and the witnesses note both the men and the manner of the record. The reformed John Gill observes that the men of Jericho were the posterity of those who formerly inhabited that city; they began where Eliashib and the priests had ended and carried the work on from thence. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the wording and the place. The recurring phrase and next unto him — literally by his hand, beside, next to — sometimes takes a singular and sometimes a plural suffix, the builders of a portion being regarded now as a company and now as individuals; here the first suffix, though singular, refers back to Eliashib and the priests, and the second to the men of Jericho. The portion these built, together with Zaccur the son of Imri, lay between the tower of Hananeel and the fish-gate in the north wall. Zaccur, they add, was the head of a family not mentioned elsewhere; and where individuals are named through this description as builders, they are to be understood as heads of houses who engaged in the work.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott dwells on the same customary phrase. Next unto him, at his hand, is used throughout the chapter to indicate the order of the building, though it involves some difficulty toward the close; as first employed here it does honour to the high priest, who must be supposed to have presided only over the religious ceremonial rather than to have laboured with his own hands. And Ellicott catches a quiet fitness in the men of Jericho building, as he notes, at the point opposite their own city — set to the stretch of wall that faced the road home to their own town.

Behind the two short notices the witnesses feel the reach of the muster. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry's larger reflection presides here, that many were active in this work who were not themselves inhabitants of Jerusalem and therefore consulted purely the public welfare and no private interest of their own; the men of Jericho stand with the first of these, coming up from their own city to labour on the capital's defence, and every Israelite, he urges, should lend a hand toward the building up of Jerusalem. The record's very form, Keil and Delitzsch note, is meant to be followed as a map — company beside company, hand by hand — so that even this bare entry, a body of Jericho men and a single unknown head of a house, takes its place as the second link in a chain the reader is to trace, unbroken, all the way round the wall and back to the sheep-gate where it began.
3:
The second gate carries the witnesses into a genuine tangle over the map of old Jerusalem. The reformed John Gill explains the name — the fish gate, so called because fish was brought through it and near it stood the fish market — but then rehearses the disagreement over where it stood: Dr. Lightfoot placed it southward, others northward, and some thought it led toward the Sea of Galilee and Jordan and all the east and north country; Gill himself judges it most likely westward, toward the Mediterranean, Tyre, and Joppa, whence fish were fetched, and reports that in Rauwolff's day a gate still stood there behind Mount Sion, called the gate of Hebron because the Hebron road passed through it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch agree it took its name from the neighbouring fish-market, to which the Syrians brought sea-fish, and note that it is mentioned again at Nehemiah 12:39, 2 Chronicles 33:14, and Zephaniah 1:10; they place it not hard against the corner tower of Hananeel but somewhat to its west in the north wall, two lengths of wall lying between. The sons of Hassenaah, they observe, built it, laying its beams — as with the like phrase at Nehemiah 2:8 — and setting up its doors, locks, and bars.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott has the fish enter rather from the Jordan and Galilee, and marks a small irregularity: contrary to the custom of the chapter, the names of the sons of Hassenaah are not given. He renders the closing terms with care — the locks and bars are better the crossbars and the catches that held them at the two ends, a rendering he carries through several later verses.

Against all this topographical confidence the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enters a blunt caution. We really know scarcely anything about these gates, he says — what they were, why so named, or where in the wall they stood; all plans of Jerusalem, its temple, walls, and gates are mere works of conjecture, and yet, he adds tartly, how learnedly have some men written upon all these subjects. The witnesses thus leave the verse in an honest tension. Gill and the grammatical-historical school will locate the fish gate as best the evidence allows, weighing west against north and citing the other Scriptures that name it; Clarke stands back and warns that such precision outruns what can be known. What none of them doubts is the plain sense of the record: a whole gate, beams and doors and bars, raised up by one family of the returned, taking its place in the northern wall next the stretch the men of Jericho had built.
4:
With the fish gate finished the register turns to a run of names who strengthened the wall between the gates, and the witnesses fasten first on a single verb. The reformed John Gill observes that this part of the wall was not wholly demolished but only weakened, and therefore the builders did not rebuild it but repaired and strengthened it — a distinction, he notes, that the same word will carry all through the chapter that follows. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm it: the term rendered repaired means properly to strengthen, that is, to make good the gaps and holes in the wall, as again at v.9 and v.27. So the three men named here — Meremoth the son of Urijah of the house of Koz, Meshullam the son of Berechiah, and Zadok the son of Baana — each took in hand a length that needed mending rather than raising anew.

Keil and Delitzsch add what is known of the men. Meremoth would repair a second portion further on, at v.21, one of several builders who took a double share. Meshullam the son of Berechiah was a person of consideration in Jerusalem, as appears from Nehemiah 6:18, where his standing and his family connections are noted. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply seals the philological point with which the verse opened: repaired is literally strengthened, whereas of the gates it had been said that they built — the gates raised from their ruins, the walls between them merely made good.

The witnesses find in that small difference of words a truer picture of the ruin the returned exiles faced. Not every stone was thrown down; much of the wall stood, breached and weakened, needing hands to close its gaps rather than to lay it afresh from the foundation. That Meremoth, one of those who strengthened here, should come back for a second stretch at v.21 is, in Keil and Delitzsch's reading, a mark of the willing spirit that ran through the work, some undertaking more than their own portion where they saw the need. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers such men into his rule for the whole chapter, that what is to be done for the public good every one should further to the utmost of his place and power, some taking more and some less as their ability allowed; united force will conquer what no single hand dares venture, and many hands make light work. Meremoth, Meshullam, and Zadok are named for their honour, three heads of houses closing the gaps in the wall beside the gate the sons of Hassenaah had built.
5:
Here for the first and only time the record notes a refusal, and the witnesses gather in unanimous reproach of the nobles of Tekoa. The reformed John Gill marks plainly that the Tekoites were the inhabitants of Tekoa, a city of Judah, and that they repaired next to the men before them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the stinging clause, that their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord: the expression, they show, is drawn from bringing the neck under a yoke, as at Jeremiah 27:11, so that to bring the neck to the service is to subject oneself to it; the nobles would not stoop to the yoke. They add that the Tekoites do not appear among those who returned with Zerubbabel, and that these same men repaired a second portion, at v.27.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls the verse remarkable on three counts: it introduces men of Tekoah not named among Zerubbabel's returned; it furnishes the solitary instance of internal opposition to the building; and it terms the common labour the work of the Lord. Yet the ordinary people of the place, he notes, did double duty, as the later verse shows. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley probes the nobles' motive — they did not submit to it nor further it, whether through sloth or covetousness or a secret compliance with the enemies of the Jews — and presses why the work was called their Lord's: it was God's, both because it had proceeded thus far by his singular providence, and because it was done for the defence of the city, the people, and the temple of God. For this, Wesley says, they are branded to all posterity; and he turns it to a maxim, that let not nobles think anything beneath them by which they may benefit their country, for what is their nobility good for but that it places them in a higher and larger sphere of usefulness.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same disdain, that the nobles would not come under the yoke of an obligation to this service, as if the dignity and liberty of their peerage were their discharge from serving God and doing good — which are indeed the highest honour and the truest freedom. The witnesses do not divide, and their shared verdict has an edge the more pointed because the common Tekoites shamed their own lords: the plain people took a first share here and a second at v.27, provoked, Henry thinks, by their nobles' bad example to a double diligence, that by their zeal they might either shame or atone for the covetousness of those set over them. One refusal, set among so many willing hands, is remembered to the nobles' lasting reproach.
6:
The old gate draws the witnesses back into the uncertain topography of the city, and again they own how little can be fixed. The reformed John Gill gathers the guesses: some think it so called because it led to the old city of Salem; Dr. Lightfoot took it for the second or third gate; Vatablus made it the gate of the old pool; or, Gill suggests, it may rather be the gate of the old wall that Josephus speaks of, leading toward the north of the land. The two men who repaired it, Jehoiada the son of Paseah and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah, laid its beams and set up its doors, its locks, and its bars, as the gate-builders did throughout. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that the old gate is nowhere else mentioned, and is probably the gate of Damascus; though, by a conjectural change in the pointing of the text, it has been rendered rather the gate of the old wall, as if set in distinction from the broad wall named a little later.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns from the map to the men, noting that here two persons joined in repairing the old gate and so were co-founders, sharing the honour of it between them. The good work we cannot compass alone, he reflects, we must be thankful to those who will go partners with us in; and he too passes on the old tradition that this gate was called the old gate because it belonged to the ancient Salem, said to have been first built by Melchizedek.

The witnesses thus leave the old gate half in shadow, its very name a puzzle — whether it looks back to Salem and Melchizedek, or marks the gate of an older wall, or is simply the Damascus gate under another title. What is plain is the labour and the fellowship. Where the sons of Hassenaah had raised the fish gate as a single family, this gate was the joint undertaking of two heads of houses, and the record keeps both their names. Henry's reflection gives the fact its weight: a general good work is furthered when men are willing to be yoked together in it, neither grudging a partner the shared credit nor waiting to do alone what two may do the better. The old gate, whatever its history, stands in the wall as the fruit of that partnership — beams, doors, locks, and bars set up by Jehoiada and Meshullam together, the next link past the length that Meremoth, Meshullam, and Zadok had strengthened.
7:
The circuit passes to men of the Benjamite towns north of the city, and to a phrase that has divided interpreters. The reformed John Gill sets the builders in their places: Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite, with the men of Gibeon and Mizpah, both towns of the tribe of Benjamin, one man belonging to the one and the other to the other. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make Melatiah the superintendent of the Gibeonites and Jadon of the men of Mizpah; Meronoth, named only here and at 1 Chronicles 27:30, must have lain near Mizpah, which they take for the modern Nebi Samwil, two leagues north-east of Jerusalem, comparing Joshua 19:26. Then comes the crux — that these built unto the throne of the governor on this side the river. Keil and Delitzsch read it as a fuller description of the men, marking them as belonging to the jurisdiction of the Pechah beyond the river, so that the verse brings to light how even Jews not under Nehemiah's authority took part in restoring the wall.

The wesleyan-arminian and grammatical-historical witnesses take the throne rather as a place. Adam Clarke reads it as the governor's house, where he dispensed justice and judgment, and adds the history: before Nehemiah's day Jerusalem was governed by a deputy from the Persian king, as Nehemiah 5:15 shows, though afterward the people were ruled by governors and judges chosen from among themselves. Charles Ellicott makes it the seat of the pechah of the whole district on this side the Euphrates, his residence when he came to Jerusalem; and John Wesley, to the same effect, the place where the governor of the country on this side Euphrates, under the Persian kings, sometimes kept a palace or throne.

So a real difference runs beneath the verse — whether the throne of the governor describes the builders' allegiance, marking them as men under the Persian pechah beyond the river, or names a physical seat of government to which their length of wall reached. Keil and Delitzsch lean to the former, Clarke, Ellicott, and Wesley to the latter. Yet the witnesses converge on what the notice reveals: that the restoration drew help from beyond the little circle of Jerusalem's own citizens, men of Gibeon and Mizpah coming up from their Benjamite towns to labour on the capital, some of them owning a jurisdiction other than Nehemiah's. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers them with the men of Jericho as builders who were not inhabitants of Jerusalem and so consulted purely the public good; the wall rose, that is, by the willing hands of a wider people than the city alone.
8:
Craftsmen now take their turn at the wall, and the witnesses read in them both the dignity of honest trades and a knot in the text. The reformed John Gill names Uzziel the son of Harhaiah of the goldsmiths — the Tzorephim, a family or guild so called from their trade — and Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke observes that from the remotest period the Jews had artists in every elegant and ornamental trade, and that goldsmiths, apothecaries, and merchants were plainly formed into companies by Nehemiah's day; the apothecaries, he adds, were rather such as dealt in drugs, aromatics, and spices, whether for embalming or for furnishing the temple with the incense consumed there. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the point a lesson: these honest tradesmen did not think their callings excused them, nor plead that they could not leave their shops for the public business, knowing that what they lost would be made up by the blessing of God upon their labour.

The tangle lies in the clause that follows, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch judge the broad wall to be a length of wall between the tower of the furnaces and the gate of Ephraim, named also at Nehemiah 12:38, rather than a single broad spot. But Charles Ellicott and John Wesley wrestle with the verb itself. Ellicott notes that the word rendered fortified means literally left, and yields a good sense so read — they left Jerusalem untouched as far as a portion of wall that needed no restoration; the gate of Ephraim stood in this stretch, as Nehemiah 12:39 shows, and it is significant that nothing is said of its rebuilding. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the common rendering but presses its force: it is not said they repaired but that they fortified it, either because this part was less demolished and needed only strengthening, or to mark their extraordinary care in making it stronger than ever.

So the witnesses divide, mildly, over a single word — whether the builders left a sound stretch alone or fortified it beyond its former strength — and they notice together the curious silence about the gate of Ephraim, which the register nowhere accounts for. What they do not doubt is the honour of the men. The goldsmith and the apothecary, whose hands were trained to fine and delicate work, turned them to the rough labour of the wall; and the record keeps their trades as a title of honour, that the ornamental crafts of the city lent their strength, no less than priests and rulers, to the common defence of Jerusalem.
9:
A ruler now takes his place among the builders, and the witnesses use his title to open a small question about the city's divisions. The reformed John Gill sets Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, and explains that the city belonged partly to Judah and partly to Benjamin, one part under a governor of Judah — as this man seems to have been — and the other under one of Benjamin. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way: the city was probably divided into two parts, one for Judah and the other for Benjamin, each with its proper governor; Rephaiah ruled the one, and Shallum, named at v.12, the other, while yet other rulers governed particular country or village districts. John Wesley draws the comparison further, that as Rome was anciently divided into quarters or regions, so was Jerusalem, and especially into two parts, one in Benjamin nearest the temple and the other in Judah, with two several rulers, both under the chief governor of the city.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dissent in a point of geography. The half part of Jerusalem, they hold, is not half the city itself but the district of country belonging to Jerusalem; they compare v.19 with v.15, where Mizpah and the district of Mizpah are likewise distinguished, so that a ruler of the half part governs a rural circuit rather than half the town. They pass on to the neighbouring builders — Jedaiah the son of Harumaph, who repaired opposite his own house, and Hattush the son of Hashabniah, of whom it cannot be determined whether he is the priest of that name at Nehemiah 10:5, the descendant of David at Ezra 8:2, or neither.

So the witnesses divide over what the half part means — the city cloven between Judah and Benjamin, each with its governor, or a landward district administered from Jerusalem. Gill, Clarke, and Wesley hold the former, Keil and Delitzsch the latter. But the difference does not touch the verse's plainer sense, on which all agree: that the rulers of the people, no less than the priests and the tradesmen, set their own hands to the wall. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers such men into his reflection on the chapter, that several rulers both of Jerusalem and of other cities were active in this work, thinking themselves bound in honour to do the utmost their wealth and power enabled for the furtherance of a good work — and that they are called rulers of but a part, or the half part, perhaps because the Persian government would trust no one man with a whole strong city, but set two as a watch upon each other.
10:
The register comes to a man who mended the wall at his own doorstep, and the witnesses find in that homely fact a quiet principle. The reformed John Gill notes that Jedaiah the son of Harumaph repaired the part of the wall that stood right against his house; to take this share he could hardly object, and it might reasonably be thought he would repair it well and make it strong, for his own safety's sake. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place him and his neighbour Hattush the son of Hashabniah in the sequence, and then look ahead to the second section that follows, repaired by Malchijah the son of Harim and Hashub the son of Pahath-Moab — two families that had come up with Zerubbabel, as Ezra 2:6 and Ezra 2:32 record.

Keil and Delitzsch pause over a difficulty in that next phrase, the other piece. Following Bertheau, some take it to mean a second section added by builders who had already repaired a first; and indeed several men in this chapter do take a double share — Meremoth at v.4 and again at v.21, the Tekoites at v.5 and v.27, and others besides. But since no first portion by Malchijah and Hashub is named, Bertheau infers that the text has not kept its original fullness, and that some statement about the gate of Ephraim and its neighbourhood, once standing before v.8, has dropped out. So Keil and Delitzsch leave the phrase honestly open, a hint that the copied list may here be defective.

The deeper note the witnesses sound is the one Jedaiah's stretch supplies. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes it a rule for the whole work: of several it is said that they repaired over against their houses, and each should apply himself to that part of a general good work which falls nearest him and lies within his reach. If every one will sweep before his own door, he says, the street will be clean; if every one will mend one, we shall all be mended. Jedaiah, repairing the wall that faced his own dwelling, is the first and plainest instance of that homely wisdom — a man who did his part by doing what lay at hand, and did it the more carefully because his own house sheltered behind it. The witnesses thus read the verse as small but exemplary: the wall rose fastest where every man took the length before his own door, and the safety of the whole was knit together out of each one's care for his own.
11:
A second stretch of wall and the tower of the furnaces fall to two families of the old return, and the witnesses attend chiefly to a recurring phrase. The reformed John Gill notes that the fathers of Malchijah the son of Harim and Hashub the son of Pahath-moab were heads of families that had come out of the captivity with Zerubbabel, so that these were men of ancient and honourable stock in the restored community. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the other piece as that which was left by Jedaiah after he had repaired the wall opposite his own house; and he offers a shrewd conjecture, that some of the principal people were obliged to repair the parts of the wall opposite their own dwellings, and that perhaps this was the general rule of the work.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes up the same expression with more caution. The phrase the other piece, he grants, occurs a few times where the repairers have already been named as mending a first piece; but it occurs several times too where there is no such earlier mention, and in those cases — as here — it must mean only what the margin indicates, a second measure, in relation to what had just been referred to, rather than a second portion by the same builders. So Ellicott gently checks the assumption that every other piece implies a builder returning for a further share; sometimes it marks no more than the next measured length along the wall.

The witnesses do not divide sharply, but they weigh the phrase differently — Clarke supposing a first portion left unnamed by Jedaiah, Keil and Delitzsch (in their comment gathered under the preceding verse) suspecting a gap in the copied text, and Ellicott content to read it as simply the next measure. What holds them together is the object of the labour: not a gate this time but the tower of the furnaces, one of the standing works of the city's defence, taken in hand by two houses of the returned. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry's rule for the chapter covers them, that what is to be done for the public good every one should further to the utmost of his place and power, some undertaking more and some less as their ability allowed. Malchijah and Hashub, heads of families that had shared the first hard journey home under Zerubbabel, now shared the harder labour of the wall, closing a second length and rebuilding a tower — their names kept in the record, like all the rest, for the honour of hands that did not spare themselves in the work of their Lord.
12:
The other ruler of Jerusalem now appears, and with him a company the witnesses greet with peculiar warmth — his daughters. The reformed John Gill names Shallum the son of Hallohesh, so called, he reports from Ben Melech, either from being an enchanter of serpents or, more kindly, a wise and prudent counsellor; and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the same double sense, son of the Enchanter, one thought skilled to charm serpents, adding that he ruled the other half part of the city, on which see v.9. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make Shallum ruler of the other half district of Jerusalem, and are careful with the pronoun: he and his daughters can only refer to Shallum himself, not to a district whose daughters would be its villages.

That very reading — daughters as villages — is the one the witnesses rise to reject. Charles Ellicott records that some have thought the daughters here to be the villages of the district Shallum governed, but he sets the notion aside as needless: the women of Jerusalem might do voluntarily what, as females, they were not pressed to do. John Wesley agrees that these were his own daughters, either heiresses or rich widows, who caused part of the work to be done at their charges. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on them with evident pleasure: some ladies, he says, are spoken of as helping forward this work — Shallum and his daughters — who, though not capable of personal labour, yet having their portions in their own hands, or being rich widows, contributed money for buying materials and paying the workmen. He recalls how Paul speaks of good women that laboured with him in the gospel, at Philippians 4:3.

So the witnesses unite, against the drier reading, to keep the daughters real. Whether Shallum's name hints at a charmer of serpents or a shrewd counsellor is a curiosity Gill and Clarke merely pass on; but that his daughters had a hand — or a purse — in the building they will not let be dissolved into a note about outlying villages. The wall, they find, was raised not by priests and rulers and tradesmen only, but by women too, who gave what they could of means where they could not give strength, and whose voluntary offering the sacred record was careful to preserve. It is a small window, the witnesses feel, upon the breadth of the willing spirit that moved the whole city: even the daughters of a ruler would not stand idle while the walls of Jerusalem lay open, but found their own way to further the work of their Lord.
13:
The valley gate and a long reach of wall to the south fall to a company from a country town, and the witnesses fix the place and measure the work. The reformed John Gill names Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah as its builders, referring back to the valley gate already noticed in the narrative. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch locate it in the west, near the present Jaffa gate — the site, on the ridge by the citadel, where an entrance provided with gates seems almost always to have stood — and take Hanun for the chief or ruler of the men of Zanoah, now Zanna, in the Wady Ismail west of Jerusalem, comparing Joshua 15:34. They built and set up its doors, its locks, and its bars, as at v.6; and the further clause, a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung gate, still depends, they insist against Bertheau, on the same verb of repairing that governs the verse.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds only that Zanoah was a town in the tribe of Judah, again citing Joshua 15:34. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lingers over the thousand cubits. So large a stretch, he observes, was not so much built as strengthened; the round number marks a comparatively wide space that had probably suffered less damage than the gates and their neighbourhoods, and therefore needed less repairing. A thousand cubits of standing wall, breached here and there, could be made good far more quickly than a ruined gate raised afresh.

The witnesses read the verse, then, as a study in the uneven ruin of the city and the uneven labour it required. Where a gate had to be wholly rebuilt, beams and doors and bars set up from the ground, a length of curtain-wall between the gates might only need its gaps closed; and so a single company from Zanoah could take both a gate and a thousand cubits of wall beside it, the one a heavy and skilled labour, the other a broad but lighter mending. The men of Zanoah, coming up like the men of Jericho and Gibeon from their own town, stand as another instance of the wider people lending its hands to Jerusalem — the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names them among those not themselves inhabitants of the city who yet consulted its welfare. From the valley gate their work ran a full thousand cubits south to the dung gate, the next in the circuit, binding the western wall to the southern in one long willing stretch.
14:
The dung gate, humblest in the circuit, is raised by a ruler from outside the city, and the witnesses pause over both the builder's name and his district. The reformed John Gill weighs whether Malchiah the son of Rechab was one of the Rechabites, who were forbidden to build houses; even so, he reasons, though they might not build private houses to dwell in, they might well be employed in building walls and fortresses for the public security — though he thinks it more probable that this man was not of that family at all. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the name otherwise. Adam Clarke fixes only the district, Beth-haccerem, a town he places in Benjamin and connects with Jeremiah 6:1; and Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical witness, cuts the knot Gill had loosened: son of Rechab, he says, does not mean a son in the sense of a Rechabite, but simply names the man's father, while part of Beth-haccerem denotes the district around that place.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes Beth-haccerem for a town or territory whose government was divided between two persons — the same arrangement the chapter shows at other places, where a man is called ruler of but a part or the half part of his city. Malchiah, ruler of one part of Beth-haccerem, came up from his own district to build the dung gate; he built it and set up its doors, its locks, and its bars, as the other gate-builders did.

The witnesses find a quiet dignity in so lowly a gate being given such care. The dung gate, through which the city's refuse was carried out, was no less a part of the wall for its mean use, and it was raised with the same beams and doors and bars as the sheep gate through which the sacrifices came. That a ruler should leave his own district of Beth-haccerem to build it is, in the witnesses' eyes, of a piece with the whole spirit of the chapter, in which rulers thought themselves bound in honour to do the utmost for a good work, and men came from the towns round about to labour on the capital's defence. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers such rulers of a part into his reflection that the Persian government would trust no one man with a whole city but set two over each, so that Beth-haccerem, like Jerusalem and Mizpah and Beth-zur, had its divided rule — yet its ruler, undivided in zeal, came to build even the gate of dung.
15:
The fountain gate and the works about the pool of Siloah draw the witnesses into the tenderest topography of the chapter, where the wall skirts the king's garden and the old city of David. The reformed John Gill names the gate of the fountain, referring to its earlier notice, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give its builder as Shallun the son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah. To the verb of building they note is added another word, he covered it — to shade or roof it over, answering to the laying of beams at v.3 and v.6 — probably a covering of beams over the gateway. The gate's position, they add, is fixed by the adjoining wall Shallun also repaired: the wall of the pool of Shelach, or Siloah, by the king's garden.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke identifies the pool of Siloah with the pool named in the gospels, and explains the stairs that go down from the city of David: Jerusalem being built on very uneven ground, with some hills taken within the walls, there was need in different places of steps by which to ascend and descend — like, he says, what one sees in the city of Bristol. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fills in the water-works. The pool of Siloah, called before the king's pool, received its water through a long subterranean conduit and supplied the king's gardens; the covering of the gate he takes, like Keil and Delitzsch, for the laying of beams, as at v.3 and v.6; and the stairs he sets on the steep sides of Ophel, of which traces are thought still to remain. From this point, he candidly warns, it becomes very hard to trace the exact course of the wall.

The witnesses thus bring the reader to the loveliest and least certain quarter of the circuit — the spring, the pool, the king's garden, the ancient stairs of David's city climbing the flank of Ophel. Here the wall did more than shut out an enemy; it enclosed the living water and the royal gardens that had been the glory of old Jerusalem. Shallun, coming from Mizpah to build, took not only the fountain gate but the difficult reach of wall that held the pool and its conduit, roofing his gate and repairing the ancient works together. That the witnesses grow uncertain of the line just here — Ellicott owning it hard to follow, Clarke likening the stepped streets to a city of his own day — only deepens the sense that the record is carrying us over real and broken ground, the very stairs and walls that David's city had known, now made good again by the willing hands of the return.
16:
A namesake of the governor himself now takes up the work, and the wall reaches the resting-place of the ancient kings. The reformed John Gill names Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, ruler of the half part of Beth-zur, a strong fortified place in Judah. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that from this verse onward the record mostly says after him rather than next unto him, and carry his stretch of wall as far as opposite the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty. The sepulchres of David, they explain, are the tombs of the house of David in the city of David, as at 2 Chronicles 32:33; the length ran along the eastern side of Zion, where there was probably an entrance to the royal burying-place.

Over the pool and the house the wesleyan-arminian and grammatical-historical witnesses agree in substance. Adam Clarke, following Calmet, takes the pool that was made for the reservoir Hezekiah made when besieged by Sennacherib, at 2 Chronicles 32:4, and the house of the mighty for a place where a band of soldiers was kept, or the city guard. Charles Ellicott concurs — the pool may be Hezekiah's reservoir of Isaiah 22:11, and the house of the mighty the barracks of David's elect troops of 1 Chronicles 11:10. John Wesley too makes the pool Hezekiah's work, at 2 Kings 20:20, distinguished thereby from a natural pool, and the house of the valiant a lodging appointed of old for the chief captains who attended the king in their courses.

The witnesses feel the weight of the ground the wall here touches — the graves of David's line, the pool of the great king who defied Assyria, the quarters of the mighty men. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks with interest that this builder is a namesake of the governor, a second Nehemiah, and raises the question the reader is bound to ask: did the great Nehemiah himself repair no particular piece? Henry answers that though he undertook no length of his own, he did more than any, for he had the oversight of them all, walking the rounds, directing and encouraging the builders, setting his hand where he saw occasion, and keeping watch upon the enemy, as the next chapter shows at Nehemiah 4:16 — the pilot, he says, needs not haul at a rope, it is enough for him to steer. So the verse joins two Nehemiahs, one building his stretch by the tombs of the kings, the other overseeing the whole; and the wall, running past the sepulchres of David and the pool of Hezekiah, gathers up the memory of the city's greatest days even as it is raised again.
17:
The circuit now comes round toward the temple, and the Levites take up the wall. The reformed John Gill names the first of them, Rehum the son of Bani, one of that tribe, as was the man who follows. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the company in order: after the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani, repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part — that is, on behalf of his district. And they carry the sequence forward to the neighbouring builders, Ezer the ruler of Mizpah at v.19, whose length lay opposite the ascent to the armoury at the turning of the wall, the armoury being probably situated on the east side of Zion where the wall formed an angle.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the significance of the place the record has reached: the circuit is coming round to the Temple, and it is fitting that here the Levites should appear, the ministers of the house whose walls the wall now approaches. Rehum the son of Bani, he notes, had the Levites under him as a body; and the phrase in his part points forward to the other part of the Keilah district — now the village of Kila — which the next verse will assign to a second ruler.

The witnesses read the verse as a turning of the whole design. Priests had begun the work at the sheep gate; tradesmen and rulers and country-folk had carried it round the north and west and south; and now, as the line bends back toward the sanctuary on the east, the Levites, the temple's own servants, take their share of the wall that guards their house. That Keilah, like Jerusalem and Beth-zur and Beth-haccerem, should have its rule divided between two men — Hashabiah over the one half here, and his brother over the other at v.18 — fits the pattern the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry drew across the chapter, that many were called rulers of but the half part of their cities, perhaps because the Persian power would trust no single man with a whole district, but set two as a watch upon each other. So the wall by the temple was raised by the temple's ministers and the rulers of a Judean town, each taking the length that fell to him, and the record keeps their names as it kept the priests' and the goldsmiths', that no rank of the people should be forgotten who put a hand to the work of their Lord.
18:
The work of Keilah is completed by its second half, and the witnesses, few here, attend to the plain sense of a brotherhood in labour. The reformed John Gill takes the brethren who repaired after him to be either the brethren of the two men just named in particular, or, following Jarchi, the Levites their brethren in general — the same sacred tribe carrying the wall on where their fellows had left it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch name their head: their brethren are the inhabitants of the second half of Keilah, under the rule of Bavai the son of Henadad, the ruler of that other half part of the district. So the two halves of the one town, governed by two men, join their hands upon two neighbouring lengths of the same wall.

The witnesses feel in this doubling the deliberate design the chapter has shown from the first. Keilah, like Jerusalem before it and Beth-zur after, is a city whose rule is divided; and where its government is halved, its labour on the wall is halved too, Hashabiah bringing up the men of the one part at v.17 and Bavai the men of the other here. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry's reflection presides over the pair: several rulers, both of Jerusalem and of other cities, were active in this work, thinking themselves bound in honour to do the utmost their place and power enabled; and they are called rulers of a part, or the half part, of their cities, perhaps because the Persian government would not trust any one man with a strong city but appointed two to be a watch upon each other — as Rome, he recalls, had its two consuls.

The brevity of the notice is itself a kind of eloquence. The record does not linger over Bavai or his men; it simply sets down that the brethren of the first company came after them and took the next measure, so that the whole district of Keilah, both its halves, is accounted for in the wall. That is the pattern the witnesses see everywhere in the chapter — no gap left, no length unclaimed, each town and family and brotherhood taking up the stone where the last had laid it down. The men of Keilah, whether Levites of one house or the townsmen of two rulers, are gathered here into the single great labour, brother beside brother upon the wall of God's city; and the record honours their unremarkable faithfulness by keeping their place in the unbroken line that runs from the sheep gate round toward the temple and home again.
19:
The wall by the temple reaches a strong point — the armoury at the angle — and the witnesses gather about the defences of the eastern ridge. The reformed John Gill names Ezer the son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, taking him to govern either another Mizpah or the other half of the town already named. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the place: Ezer repaired another piece opposite the ascent to the armoury of the angle; the word rendered armoury is an abbreviation of the fuller term for arsenal, and the angle is a genitive, so that the phrase means the armoury standing at the turning of the wall. They locate it on the east side of Zion, where the city wall formed an angle, or at a corner within the city where no other buildings adjoined it on the south.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the going up to the armoury as either a tower that defended the angle where two walls met, or the city arsenal itself, where shields and spears and the like were kept to arm the people in a time of danger. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase literally, the armoury of the corner, and sets it at the north-west corner of the city of David, with its own special wall — one of the fortified turnings where the line of the wall changed direction and a store of weapons was kept ready.

The witnesses read the verse as marking a place of strength in the circuit, where the wall bent at an angle and an armoury guarded the turning. The very difficulty of fixing its exact site — whether tower or arsenal, at this corner or that — does not obscure its plain function: here was a point where weapons were stored and the wall's line broke, a spot the defenders would need to hold. Ezer, ruler of Mizpah, took the length opposite this armoury, a second portion added to his labour, tying the temple wall to the strong angle of Zion. The witnesses feel, as Ellicott confessed a little earlier, that the course of the wall grows hard to trace just here; yet the record presses on turning by turning, naming the ruler, the armoury, and the angle, so that the reader may follow the eastern defences of the city of David as they rose again under the willing hands of the returned, arsenal and corner and all.
20:
One builder is singled out for the spirit in which he worked, and the witnesses dwell on his zeal. The reformed John Gill notes that Baruch the son of Zabbai earnestly repaired the other piece — the word, he says, meaning in anger, as though the man were angry with himself or with others at the backwardness shown to the work, and therefore attended to it with all the haste and eagerness imaginable. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the rare word carefully. Bertheau would emend it to read up the hill, but they reject the change: the term cannot here mean to be angry, but may without difficulty be taken in the sense of to emulate or to contend, as at Jeremiah 22:15 and Jeremiah 12:5, so that Baruch emulously repaired his portion, striving to outdo his fellows in diligence.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the same fervour. Adam Clarke says simply that Baruch distinguished himself by his zeal and activity; John Wesley, that he did his work with eminent diligence and fervency, a thing noted to his commendation, and that it is probable this good man's zeal provoked many others to take the more pains and make the more haste. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns a small puzzle in the scene — the reason of this man's emulation in building near the high priest's house does not appear — for Baruch's stretch ran from the turning of the wall unto the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest.

The witnesses do not divide over the man's ardour, only over the shade of the word — whether Baruch worked in a holy anger at others' sloth, or in a generous rivalry to excel — and the weight of them, with Keil and Delitzsch, falls on emulation rather than wrath. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers him into the chapter's honour-roll as the one of whom it is said that he earnestly repaired his share, doing it with an inflamed zeal — not that the others were cold or indifferent, but that he was the most vigorous of any and so made himself remarkable. It is good, Henry reflects, to be thus zealously affected in a good thing; and he too judges that this good man's example quickened his neighbours to greater pains. So the record, which elsewhere keeps only names and lengths, pauses over Baruch to mark the temper of his heart, and the witnesses read in that single adverb a whole portrait of a man who could not build the wall of his God by halves.
21:
A builder already met with returns for a second stretch, and the witnesses note both his double diligence and the house his work now reached. The reformed John Gill observes that Meremoth the son of Uriah, the son of Koz, had wrought before in another part, at v.4, but having finished that, he sets his hand a second time to the work, taking now the length from the door of the house of Eliashib even to the end of it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the second portion and carry the record on to the priests who followed — the men of the plain, or, as they read it, of the district of the Jordan, the kikkar, taking the word not for the country round Jerusalem but for the Jordan valley, as at Nehemiah 12:28 and Genesis 13:10; so priests, they infer, were then dwelling in the valley near Jericho.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse simply, that Meremoth added to his earlier labour the repair of the wall under this house; and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley catches a small domestic detail in the wording — that Meremoth built from the door of the house to the end of it, so that the door was not in the middle of the house, as they commonly are now, but at one end.

The witnesses find in Meremoth an instance of the willing spirit the chapter loves to record — a man who, having done his own share, took up another where he saw the need. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws him into the rule that closes his survey: some of those that had first done helped their fellows, and undertook another share where there was most need; Meremoth repaired at v.4 and again here, as the Tekoites did at v.5 and v.27. Such men, Henry reflects, were not content to have borne their own burden, but where others were slack or where the work pressed, they set their hands afresh; and the record keeps their double labour to their honour. So Meremoth's name, appearing twice in the one chapter, becomes a quiet emblem of the whole: a wall raised not by men who did the least their portion required, but by some at least who did more than was asked, closing gap after gap until the circuit was whole. The stretch he took ran the length of the high priest's own house, binding the temple quarter tighter into the line of the wall.
22:
The priests of the surrounding country take their turn, and the witnesses divide gently over where their homes lay. The reformed John Gill takes the men of the plain to be priests dwelling either in the plain of Jericho, where in later times at least there was a station of the priests, or in the plain about Jerusalem, who also lent their help to the repair of the wall. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets them in the country round the city: some of the officers of the temple, particularly the singers, dwelt in the plain about Jerusalem, as Nehemiah 12:28 shows, and it is likely that several of the priests dwelt in the same place. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it rather of the Jordan valley — the men of the plain are priests dwelling in the Kikkar of Scripture, the deep valley of the Jordan.

So a small difference runs beneath the verse, whether the plain means the level country immediately about Jerusalem, where the singers and priests had their villages, or the far Jordan valley near Jericho. Gill allows either; Clarke inclines to the nearer plain; Ellicott, with the grammatical-historical reading gathered under the preceding verse, holds firmly to the kikkar of the Jordan. The difference is one of geography only, and the witnesses do not press it to a quarrel.

What they agree in is the honour of the thing. Priests who did not live within the walls, whose homes lay out in the open country — whether by Jericho or in the villages about the city — came up to labour on Jerusalem's defence, as the men of Jericho and Gibeon and Zanoah had done before them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers them with those active in the work who were not themselves inhabitants of Jerusalem, and therefore consulted purely the public welfare and no private interest of their own. That the temple's ministers should come in from their country dwellings to build is, in the witnesses' eyes, of a piece with the whole spirit of the return: every Israelite, wherever he lived, was to lend a hand toward the building up of Jerusalem, and these rural priests would not be absent from the work merely because their homes were spared the danger. Their names are not given, only their office and their country; but the record keeps them, a company of the plain, faithful upon the wall that guarded the sanctuary they served.
23:
The wall now passes the very houses of its builders, and the witnesses mark again the men who repaired at their own doors. The reformed John Gill notes only that the after him of the verse follows upon the last of the priests just named, joining this length to theirs. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set down the builders and own how little is known of them: Benjamin and Hashub repaired over against their house, and Azariah the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ananiah, by his house — three men of whom nothing further can be said, save that each built the wall that stood before his own dwelling. They carry the sequence on to Binnui the son of Henadad, who took the next piece from the house of this Azariah to the turning of the wall.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the recurring phrase a lesson, as he had at v.10: of several it is said that they repaired over against their houses, and when a general good work is to be done, each should apply himself to that part which falls nearest him and lies within his reach. If every man will mend one, he says, we shall be all mended; and if he that has but a chamber will repair before that, he does his part. Benjamin, Hashub, and Azariah are three plain instances of it — men who took no distant or chosen length, but simply built the wall that sheltered their own homes, and so, each guarding his own, guarded the whole.

The witnesses read in this quiet clustering of houses along the wall a picture of the city knitting itself together for its own defence. Where the line ran past a man's dwelling, that man took it in hand; his own safety and the city's were bound in the same stones, and he had every reason to build well. The record does not need to praise Benjamin and Hashub and Azariah; it is enough that it names them and sets them at their own doors, for the naming is itself an honour, and the placing tells the whole tale. So the eastern wall rose, house by house, each householder repairing before his own dwelling, until the private care of many for their own homes had raised, without gap, the public wall of the city of God — the very pattern, the witnesses feel, of how a people's common good is best secured, when every one is faithful in the little length that lies before his door.
24:
The wall turns a corner, and the witnesses follow the line to the angle by the king's house. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Binnui the son of Henadad began where Azariah had ended, taking the next length of the wall. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace his portion from the house of Azariah to the turning of the wall, even unto the corner, and carry the record on to Palal the son of Uzai, whose stretch lay opposite the angle and the high tower that stood out from the king's house by the court of the prison. They pause over the word rendered high: it is best joined to the tower, so that we read the high tower, rather than to the king's house, for nothing is known of an upper and a lower king's house; and the same tower is called the great tower at v.27, which favours the sense high here. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the place plainly: unto the corner means the north-eastern angle of the city of David.

The witnesses read the verse as the wall's approach to the royal quarter, where the line bent sharply at the corner of David's city and a high tower rose beside the palace and its prison. The record grows dense here with turnings and towers — the angle, the corner, the projecting tower — for the eastern defences of Zion were strong and much broken, and the copyists who kept this list preserved every bend of the wall. Binnui, taking a second portion as Meremoth and the Tekoites had done, closed the length from Azariah's house to the very turning; and beyond him Palal took up the tower and the angle, so that the strong north-eastern corner of the city of David was made good stone by stone.

What the witnesses feel in these crowded notices is the fidelity of the account to the real and difficult ground. This was no smooth curtain-wall but a fortified corner, with a tower thrusting out from the palace and the prison-court beneath it; and the men who rebuilt it — Binnui the son of Henadad, and Palal after him — did their exact work at the exact place, the record keeping each turning as it kept each name. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry's rule for the whole covers them, that every one took his share, some more and some less, according to his ability, that every man might know what he had to do and mind it; and here, at the hard angle of the king's house, the sharing held, and the wall turned its corner unbroken toward the temple.
25:
The wall runs on beneath the king's palace and the tower of the prison-court, and the witnesses fix the place with care. The reformed John Gill takes Palal the son of Uzai to have dwelt over against the turning of the wall, and so to have repaired what stood right against him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set his portion opposite the turning and the tower that lieth out from the king's high house, that was by the court of the prison, and carry the record on to Pedaiah the son of Parosh who followed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase more exactly — better, the high tower outlying from the king's palace — and explains the court of the prison: the palace generally had its prison, and near this stood the prison-gate named at Nehemiah 12:39.

Keil and Delitzsch look ahead from Palal's stretch to the notice that follows, on the dwellings of the temple-servants: having reached the place where the wall encloses Ophel, the record inserts a remark that the Nethinim dwelt there, as far as opposite the water-gate toward the east and the projecting tower — the water-gate lying, as Nehemiah 12:37 shows, beyond the south-eastern corner of the temple area.

The witnesses read the verse as the wall's passage through the very heart of the old royal city — the palace, its high tower, the court where prisoners were kept. Here the defences and the dignities of the monarchy stood close together: a tower thrusting out from the king's house, a prison beneath it, a gate named for the prison hard by. Palal and Pedaiah, taking their lengths against this strong and storied quarter, rebuilt the wall where it guarded the seat of David's line. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry's reflection on the whole work bears upon them, that every one took the share that fell to him and minded it, some by their own houses and some, like these, at the great public works of the city; and the record, keeping the tower and the palace and the prison-court in view, lets the reader see that the wall of the return ran past all that remained of the ancient kingdom, binding the memory of David's house into the new defence of his city. From this point the line will pass the dwellings of the Nethinim on the slope of Ophel, and so climb toward the temple wall itself.
26:
The record pauses to notice where the temple-servants dwelt, and the witnesses read the remark as a marker of place upon the wall. The reformed John Gill sets the Nethinim in Ophel — a high part of the wall on this side — and takes them for servants to the Levites who repaired here, where their own dwellings were. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives the fullest account. It has been proposed, following the Syriac, to insert a who before dwelt, making the Nethinim builders of this stretch; but Ellicott judges this needless. Ophel, he explains, was the long rounded spur running out south of the Temple, on the sides of which the ancient temple-servants still dwelt, kept apart from others, on a tract of land reaching from the water-gate toward the east to the outlying tower of the king's citadel in the west. And he adds a careful qualification: nothing is said of their part in the general labour.

That last note opens a quiet question the witnesses do not force. Gill takes the Nethinim to have repaired the wall by their dwellings, as the householders did all along the eastern line; Ellicott is more cautious, observing that the text records only where they lived, not that they built. The verse may be, that is, no more than a landmark — the wall ran past the quarter of the Nethinim on the slope of Ophel — inserted to fix the course of the line, rather than a notice of another company of builders.

The witnesses feel the fitness of the temple-servants dwelling just here, on the spur below the sanctuary they served, between the water-gate and the king's tower. The lowest order of the house of God had its home nearest the wall that guarded the house, and the record, tracing the line round the eastern ridge, cannot pass their quarter without naming it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, following the same course, had already reached the place where the wall encloses Ophel, and read this remark on the Nethinim as the natural mark of that stretch. So the verse stands, in the witnesses' reading, as a small window upon the settled order of the restored city — priests and Levites and Nethinim each in their place, the servants of the sanctuary lodged on the holy hill — set into the register of the wall precisely where the line of building passed their dwellings on the eastern slope of Ophel, below the temple toward which the whole circuit is now bending back.
27:
The men of Tekoa appear a second time, and the witnesses turn their double labour into a rebuke of their own lords. The reformed John Gill notes that the Tekoites, having finished what they undertook in another part of the wall at v.5, now engage in this part also; and this, he says, shows their great zeal and diligence, the more remarkable because their nobles had been so backward to the work and had withdrawn from it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the place: the Tekoites repaired a second piece from opposite the great tower that standeth out to the wall of Ophel. That wall of Ophel, they add, had been much built upon — King Jotham built much on it, as 2 Chronicles 27:3 records, and Manasseh compassed Ophel with a very high wall, at 2 Chronicles 33:14, carrying it round the western, southern, and eastern sides, while on the north no wall was needed, Ophel being there protected by the southern wall of the temple area.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a small correction of the wording — after them is literally after him, referring back to Pedaiah of v.25. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the moral home. The Tekoites here are the same as before, who, having dispatched their first share sooner than their brethren, freely offered to supply the defects of others who had neglected the part committed to them; and their double diligence is noted, Wesley says, both for the greater shame of their nobles, who would do no part of the work, and for their own honour, who were so far from being corrupted by that bad example that they were quickened to a greater zeal and industry in this pious work.

The witnesses read the two appearances of the Tekoites as the chapter's sharpest contrast. Their nobles, alone in all the record, had refused the yoke of their Lord's work at v.5; the common people of the same town, so far from following that example, did not one share only but two. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the irony: their nobles set them a bad example by withdrawing from the service, which, instead of serving the people for an excuse to sit still, perhaps made them the more forward to do double work, that by their zeal they might either shame or atone for the carelessness of their nobles. So the men of Tekoa, twice named upon the wall, stand for the truest freedom the chapter knows — the willing service of those who owed nothing to their leaders' example, and gave everything to the work of God.
28:
Above the horse gate the priests take up the wall by their own houses, and the witnesses gather what is known of that gate near the temple. The reformed John Gill offers the several accounts of its name: the horse gate was so called either because near it were stables, or because through it horses were led to be watered at the brook of Kidron, to which it lay near, or to be exercised in the valley; and Josephus, he notes, speaks of a horse tower that may have stood close by. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place it near the temple and the royal palace, as appears from 2 Chronicles 23:15 compared with 2 Kings 11:6, and yet in the neighbourhood of the wall of Ophel; they seek it in the wall running over the Tyropoean valley, and note that it is mentioned again at Jeremiah 31:40.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the same sense of the name — the place through which the horses passed to be watered, near the temple — and passes on a rabbinic tradition that one might ride as far as this gate on the way to the temple, but was then obliged to alight, for a horse could go no farther; horses, he adds, were never very plentiful in Jerusalem. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the gate between the Temple and the palace, and observes that the space from the wall of Ophel seems not to have needed repair, so that the priests began their work above the gate itself.

The witnesses read the verse as another instance of the householder repairing at his own door, now among the priests who dwelt by the temple. From above the horse gate, the record says, the priests repaired, every one over against his own house — each taking the length that faced his dwelling, as the men of the eastern wall had done at v.23 and their neighbours before them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry's rule presides here too, that each should apply himself to the part of a general good work that lies nearest him; and it was fitting that the priests, whose homes clustered about the sanctuary, should build the wall that ran past their own doors near the horse gate, so that the very ministers of the house helped to gird the house with a wall, every man before his own dwelling.
29:
The wall passes the house of a priest and the post of a gatekeeper, and the witnesses attend to the two men and a nicety of identity. The reformed John Gill notes that Zadok the son of Immer repaired over against his house, beginning where the priests before him had ended and repairing as far as his house reached; and being perhaps a person of some note, his house might be a large one. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take Zadok, son of Immer, for the head of the priestly order of Immer named at Ezra 2:37. The second builder they weigh more carefully: Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate, can hardly be the same as the Shemaiah of the sons of Shechaniah entered among the descendants of David at 1 Chronicles 3:22; and the east gate, they insist, is the east gate of the temple, not to be confounded with the water-gate toward the east of v.26.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply marks the coincidence of the name — Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah is the name at 1 Chronicles 3:22 of a descendant of David — leaving open, as Keil and Delitzsch had, whether the two are one man. The keeper of the east gate, whether of David's line or no, took his place on the wall by his own post, guarding in stone the gate he guarded in office; and it is fitting, the witnesses feel, that the man charged with the sanctuary's eastern door should build the wall that ran beside it, his daily office and his day's labour falling in the same place.

The witnesses read the verse as the wall drawing very near the temple itself, past the house of a priestly chief and the station of the man who kept the sanctuary's eastern gate. Zadok repaired the length before his own house, as the priests had done above the horse gate; and Shemaiah, whose charge was the east gate of the temple, built the wall in its neighbourhood. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry's principle holds again, that each did the part nearest to his own place and calling — the head of a priestly house before his dwelling, the gatekeeper by his gate. So the record, careful even to distinguish this Shemaiah from a like-named son of David, and this east gate from the water-gate a little back, keeps the line exact as it comes round to the sanctuary, every builder set where his house or his office bound him to the wall of the city of God.
30:
A sixth son who worked where his elders held back draws the witnesses' particular notice, and with him a lodger who repaired before his chamber. The reformed John Gill marks that Hanun, though the sixth son of Zalaph, was the only one of the six who wrought at this work — a thing observed, he says, to his great commendation. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch name the builders — Hananiah the son of Shelemiah and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, and after them Meshullam the son of Berechiah over against his chamber — and note that this Meshullam can hardly be the man of the same name at v.4, who is there marked off by the addition son of Meshezabeel. The word rendered chamber, they add, occurs only here and at Nehemiah 13:7, and seems to mean his dwelling.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the lesson from Hanun's rank among his brothers: it seems his five elder brethren laid not their hands to the work, but he did; and in doing that which is good, Wesley says, we need not stay to see our betters go before us. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the same detail — that of one of these builders it is observed he was the sixth son of his father, whose five elder brethren, it seems, laid not their hands to this work, but he did — and draws it out: in doing good we need not wait for our elders to lead; if they decline it, it does not follow that we must. Thus the younger brother, Henry reflects, if he be the better man and does his generation better service, is indeed the better gentleman, for those are most honourable who are most useful.

Of Meshullam, the lodger, Henry finds a smaller instance of the same faithfulness. Where others repaired over against their houses, this one — who, it is likely, was only a lodger — repaired over against his chamber; when a general good work is to be done, each should apply himself to the part nearest him, and if he that has but a chamber will repair before that, he does his part. The witnesses thus read the verse as a double honour to the humble: a sixth son who would not wait for his elders, and a lodger with but a single room who yet took his length of the wall. The record keeps both, that neither low birth-order nor small estate might excuse a man from the work of his Lord, nor rob him of his place in its lasting register.
31:
The circuit nears its close among the guilds and the last of the gates, and the witnesses work at an obscure and crowded verse. The reformed John Gill names Malchiah the goldsmith's son — the son of Tzoreph, so called from his trade. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the title not as a proper name but as an appellative: son of the goldsmith, or better, a member of the goldsmiths' guild. His length, they own, is described in obscure terms — unto the house of the Nethinim and of the merchants, over against the gate Miphkad, and to the going up of the corner. The Masoretic pointing so divides it; the Septuagint divides otherwise, making Malchiah repair as far as the house of the Nethinim while the spice-merchants repaired opposite the gate Miphkad — a division Bertheau prefers, but which Keil and Delitzsch resist as resting on questionable grounds.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott smooths a phrase or two. The place of the Nethinim is rather the house of the Nethinim; and of the merchants he offers a shrewd guess — there may be some connection between the traders, who brought their doves and the like for the worshippers, and the Nethinim to whose house or depot they brought them. Near the sheep gate, he adds, was the going up of the corner, or an ascent to the gate Miphkad, about which nothing is known.

The witnesses leave the verse in honest half-light, its exact reading disputed between the Masoretes and the Greek, its gate Miphkad and its going up of the corner beyond certain identification. What is plain is that the wall has now come round almost to its starting-point, and that the last builders are men of the trades — a goldsmith's son, the merchants, the quarter of the Nethinim by the temple. Ellicott's conjecture, tying the merchants who sold doves to the temple-servants who received them, gives a glimpse of the living traffic of the sanctuary that clustered here by the sheep gate, through which the sacrifices came. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had noted at the first that honest tradesmen, goldsmiths and merchants no less than priests and rulers, were active in this work; and here at the end, as at the beginning, it is the craftsmen and traders of the city who close the gap, building the wall past their own guild-houses toward the corner where the whole circuit began.
32:
The last stretch is closed, and the circuit comes full round to the gate where it began. The reformed John Gill marks the completion plainly: between the going up of the corner and the sheep gate the goldsmiths and the merchants repaired — the very place where the building first began, and where it now ended. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix this last section between the upper chamber of the corner and the sheep-gate, the whole length of the east wall of the temple as far as the gate at which the description had opened, at v.1. This eastern wall, they suggest, may have suffered less at the demolition of the city by the Chaldeans, or have been partly repaired when the temple was rebuilt, so that less restoration was now needed. And they stand back to survey the whole: the enumeration, commencing and ending at the sheep-gate and joining almost every portion to the last by the words next unto or after him, gives good ground to conclude that in these forty-two sections, gates and all, we have a description of the entire fortified wall about the city, without a single gap.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the last two guilds. The word rendered goldsmiths may signify smiths, or workers in metal of any kind, though it is generally understood of those who wrought in gold; and the naming of merchants and goldsmiths, he repeats, shows that these were formed into bodies corporate in those ancient times. He notes how the old versions render the pair variously — the Vulgate as ours, goldsmiths and traders; the Syriac, goldsmiths and druggists; the Arabic, smelters of metal and porters; the Septuagint in some copies smiths and merchants — a small witness to the difficulty of the terms. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott seals the circuit: the goldsmiths and the merchants undertook the small space necessary to complete the round, up to the sheep gate.

The witnesses close the chapter where it opened, at the sheep gate through which the sacrifices came, the wall now whole about the city of God. What the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry read as the burden of the whole is fulfilled in this last verse: the work was so divided that every one knew what he had to do and minded it, without strife save which should do most for the public good, and no gap was left in the end. From the priests who hallowed the first gate to the goldsmiths and merchants who filled the last small space, the willing hands of the whole people — priests, Levites, rulers, tradesmen, countrymen, and women — had built and joined and closed the wall, so that Jerusalem stood girded again, and the circuit that began in sacrifice ended, unbroken, at the same holy gate.
